paragraphs: Training across many machines creates a tension between computation and communication. Centralized methods can make rapid optimization progress, but coordinating all machines can become a bottleneck. Existing decentralized methods avoid that central coordination yet can be slower than accelerated stochastic methods running on one machine. This paper addresses that gap for smooth, strongly convex optimization problems.

The proposed algorithm, ADFS, combines local stochastic proximal updates with randomly selected communications between pairs of machines. Its analysis uses an augmented graph to represent the optimization problem, carefully accounts for synchronization time, and extends an accelerated coordinate method to support arbitrary sampling. These components connect the algorithm’s computational progress with the cost of operating over a network.

The stated scaling result is that n machines can learn from nm samples in the time an optimal single-machine algorithm needs for m samples. This holds only up to a critical network size determined by communication delays, local sample counts, and network topology. Experiments also show improvements over existing decentralized approaches.
neurips-2019-an-accelerated-decentralize.tldr: ADFS combines accelerated local updates with pairwise communication to achieve strong distributed scaling up to a network-dependent size limit.

paragraphs: Super-resolution methods often assume a particular process converted a high-resolution image into its low-resolution input. Real images frequently depart from that assumed process, and the mismatch can substantially damage reconstruction quality. This paper tackles blind super-resolution by estimating the image’s unknown downscaling kernel from the low-resolution image itself.

KernelGAN uses the recurrence of small image patches across scales as its learning signal. It trains a separate adversarial model on the input image at test time. The generator produces a further-downscaled image, while the discriminator tries to distinguish its patches from patches in the original input. Training encourages the two patch distributions to become indistinguishable.

The trained generator supplies the image-specific downscaling operation that an existing super-resolution algorithm can then use. The method is unsupervised and needs no training images beyond the input being processed. The authors report state-of-the-art blind super-resolution results when combining this kernel estimator with existing reconstruction algorithms, demonstrating the practical value of learning how an image was downscaled.
neurips-2019-blind-super-resolution-kern.tldr: KernelGAN estimates an image’s downscaling kernel by learning recurring patch patterns within that image, improving blind super-resolution.

paragraphs: The paper studies repeated decisions in which a learner chooses groups of items and observes their relative preferences rather than absolute rewards. The goal is to keep regret small: the accumulated cost of learning while making choices. Preferences follow a Multinomial logit model, which supplies the probabilistic structure used by the algorithms and analysis.

Two feedback settings are considered. In one, the learner chooses subsets up to a maximum size and observes the ordered top m items. In the other, every chosen subset contains exactly k items, and the learner observes its complete ranking. The authors develop algorithms with instance-dependent regret scaling as O((n/m) ln T) and O((n/k) ln T), respectively.

Matching fundamental limits establish that these regret rates are optimal in order for the studied settings. The dependence on m explains the value of requesting richer rankings: observing several leading items can improve regret relative to observing only a winner. Empirical evaluations support the theoretical results, connecting the feedback advantage to the algorithms’ observed behavior.
neurips-2019-combinatorial-bandits-with-.tldr: Under a Multinomial logit preference model, ranking-based subset selection admits order-optimal regret that improves with richer feedback.

paragraphs: The paper examines correlated equilibrium in games that unfold through a sequence of decisions. An external device privately recommends moves as play progresses. Players may reject a recommendation, but doing so ends their access to future recommendations. This setup makes the timing and continuation of advice part of the strategic situation.

The authors show that an extensive-form correlated equilibrium can be represented as the solution of a bilinear saddle-point problem. They use this representation, together with structural properties of these equilibria, to develop a simple subgradient descent method. The method offers better scalability than the prior linear-programming approach, providing a computational use for the new formulation.

The paper also introduces two benchmark games covering mediation for conflict resolution and bargaining or negotiation. Studying these games reveals that equilibria maximizing social welfare can involve subtle sequential behavior. These examples therefore serve two purposes: they provide problems for evaluating future solvers and show why understanding correlated recommendations requires attention to how decisions unfold over time.
neurips-2019-correlation-in-extensive-fo.tldr: A saddle-point formulation enables a more scalable correlated-equilibrium solver and reveals subtle recommendation strategies in sequential games.

paragraphs: Cleaning training data can improve a model, but identifying which examples matter often requires substantial domain expertise. This paper proposes an automated way to identify influential training instances for models trained with stochastic gradient descent. The aim is to make useful data cleansing accessible without requiring users to supply knowledge about the data’s subject matter.

The method follows the history of training. It retraces SGD updates and incorporates the intermediate models produced along the way to infer the influence of individual examples. This approach is designed to move beyond earlier methods that require a convex loss and an already optimal model, conditions that do not always describe modern machine learning.

Experiments show that the method can accurately identify influential instances. On MNIST and CIFAR10, removing instances recommended by the method improves the resulting models. The findings support using the optimization trajectory as evidence for data-cleansing decisions: information about how a model was trained can help identify examples whose removal is beneficial in the evaluated tasks.
neurips-2019-data-cleansing-for-models-t.tldr: Retracing SGD updates helps identify influential training examples whose removal improved models in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Distributed and collaborative training commonly exchange gradients, the information used to update model parameters. This paper challenges the belief that sharing these updates keeps the underlying training examples private. It shows that publicly shared gradients can contain enough information to recover private training data, making the exchanged updates themselves a potential source of disclosure.

The authors introduce an attack called deep leakage from gradients. In the demonstrated cases, recovery takes only a few gradient steps and can reconstruct original training examples rather than merely produce similar-looking substitutes. That distinction matters because the claimed leakage concerns the actual source data, beyond a general resemblance to the kinds of examples used in training.

The attack is validated on both computer vision and natural language processing tasks. The authors empirically report stronger leakage than previous approaches and discuss possible defensive strategies. These findings establish a concrete reason to reconsider gradient-sharing safety: exchanging updates can expose data even when the training examples themselves are not directly transmitted.
neurips-2019-deep-leakage-from-gradients.tldr: Shared gradients can reveal original private training examples, as demonstrated by attacks on vision and language tasks.

paragraphs: This paper develops VQ-VAE models for generating large, detailed images. Its central move is to improve the autoregressive models that generate compressed image codes. Strengthening these learned priors and organizing the codes into a multiscale hierarchy allows the system to produce images with greater coherence and fidelity than earlier versions of the approach.

The architecture separates image encoding and decoding from sequential generation. Simple feed-forward networks perform the encoding and decoding, while the autoregressive model operates only in the compressed latent space. The authors report that this sampling process is an order of magnitude faster than generating directly in pixel space, with particular benefits for large images.

On complex datasets such as ImageNet, the hierarchical model generates samples whose quality rivals state-of-the-art generative adversarial networks. The authors also report avoiding GAN-associated problems such as mode collapse and insufficient diversity. The results show how powerful priors over compressed representations can combine high image quality, diverse outputs, and a more efficient location for the sequential sampling work.
neurips-2019-generating-diverse-high-fid.tldr: VQ-VAE-2 generates diverse, high-quality images by sampling powerful hierarchical priors in a compressed representation.

paragraphs: The paper studies Newton-based optimization for regularized convex losses in the generalized self-concordant family, including logistic and softmax regression. Its focus is on ill-conditioned problems, where optimization is sensitive to uneven curvature. The proposed scheme solves a sequence of problems whose regularization parameters gradually decrease, connecting successive optimization tasks.

The authors prove global convergence and a linear convergence rate whose constant factor grows only logarithmically with the condition number. In the parametric setting, the algorithm has the same scaling as standard first-order methods while offering improved behavior, especially for ill-conditioned problems. The result links a simple regularization schedule to a favorable dependence on conditioning.

For nonparametric learning, the scheme is combined with Nyström projections. The resulting algorithm achieves optimal generalization bounds with O(n df) time and O(df²) memory, without dependence on the condition number in these stated complexities. Here n counts observations and df denotes degrees of freedom. This extends guarantees previously available for least-squares regression to the broader loss setting studied.
neurips-2019-globally-convergent-newton-.tldr: A decreasing-regularization Newton scheme provides convergence guarantees and efficient nonparametric learning for difficult convex regression problems.

paragraphs: A deep network may represent a function efficiently without being easy to train to learn it. This paper investigates that gap between expressive power and gradient-based optimization. It asks whether the representational advantages of depth actually become available through training, using distributions with a fractal structure to make the distinction precise.

The authors show that these distributions can be represented efficiently by deep networks but not shallow ones. Their coarse-to-fine organization also exposes an important training issue: the balance between broad patterns and fine details affects whether gradient-based optimization is likely to succeed. When the distribution concentrates on fine details, the authors prove that such algorithms are likely to fail.

For at least some distributions, the resulting argument connects successful deep learning to whether shallower networks can approximate the distribution. Thus, greater expressive power alone does not establish that training will exploit it. The paper conjectures that this dependence on shallow approximability holds more generally, while its proved conclusion remains tied to the distributions covered by the analysis.
neurips-2019-is-deeper-better-only-when-.tldr: For certain fractal distributions, depth improves expressivity while gradient-based learning can fail when fine details dominate.

paragraphs: This paper generalizes k-means clustering from points to lines. The task is to select k point centers that minimize the total squared distance between each input line and its nearest center. This changes the objects being summarized while retaining the familiar goal of finding a small set of representative locations.

The main construction is a coreset: a small weighted subset of lines that approximately preserves the clustering cost for any proposed set of k centers. Using this summary, the authors obtain a (1 + ε)-approximation in O(n log n) time when the error tolerance, number of centers, and dimension are fixed constants. Preserving costs across candidate solutions makes the summary useful for optimization.

The coreset also supports one-pass distributed streaming through a merge-and-reduce procedure, with memory, update time, and communication near-logarithmic in the number of lines. Supporting deletions requires linear space. Extensions address other distance objectives and outliers, while experiments on ten cloud machines demonstrate practical performance. Together, the results connect approximation guarantees with ways to process large collections of lines.
neurips-2019-k-means-clustering-of-lines.tldr: Small weighted summaries enable provably accurate clustering of lines and efficient distributed streaming.

paragraphs: Class imbalance creates a mismatch when training data heavily favors some categories but evaluation still requires good performance on rare ones. This paper introduces two methods for that setting: a loss function that accounts for the label distribution and a training schedule that changes when class re-weighting begins.

The label-distribution-aware margin loss, or LDAM, is motivated by minimizing a margin-based generalization bound. It replaces the standard cross-entropy training objective and can be combined with existing re-weighting or re-sampling strategies. The second method postpones re-weighting until after an initial training stage, giving the model time to learn an initial representation while avoiding some complications associated with early re-weighting or re-sampling.

Experiments cover several vision benchmarks, including the real-world imbalanced iNaturalist 2018 dataset. Either method alone improves over existing techniques in the reported tests, and combining them yields larger gains. The findings suggest that both the training objective and the timing of imbalance correction can contribute to better generalization when less frequent classes matter.
neurips-2019-learning-imbalanced-dataset.tldr: A label-aware margin loss and delayed class re-weighting improve learning from imbalanced datasets, with stronger gains when combined.

paragraphs: Transfer learning often assumes access to source training data or control over how source models were trained. This paper considers a more restricted setting: several pretrained networks are available only as black-box feature extractors. The target task contains classes none of those networks has previously observed, and only a few labeled target examples are available.

The proposed method, maximal correlation weighting, combines feature functions from the source networks using tools from nonlinear maximal correlation analysis. Its purpose is to find an appropriate weighting of the available representations for the target classifier. This allows the learner to use distributed pretrained models without requiring joint source training or access to their original training samples.

The authors demonstrate effective, computationally efficient classification on datasets derived from CIFAR-100, Stanford Dogs, and Tiny ImageNet. They also use the method to characterize how valuable different source tasks are for a target task. The contribution therefore includes both a way to combine existing representations and a way to assess their relative usefulness for new classes.
neurips-2019-learning-new-tricks-from-ol.tldr: Maximal correlation weighting combines black-box pretrained features to learn new classes from very few labeled examples.

paragraphs: Few-shot learning asks a model to adapt to a task using only a small labeled support set. The unlabeled examples it must eventually predict also contain information about that task. This paper proposes using that additional information through transductive meta-learning, allowing adaptation to draw on the target inputs even though their labels are unavailable.

The framework, Self-Critique and Adapt, first trains a base model on the support set using an existing learning method. It then updates the model using a learned, label-free loss represented by a neural network. This loss is itself meta-learned so that the resulting adaptation improves generalization, providing an update signal when ordinary label-dependent training cannot be applied to the target set.

Experiments show substantially better generalization than baselines that adapt only on labeled support examples, with state-of-the-art performance reported. The central contribution is a mechanism for learning how to use unlabeled task information during adaptation. It expands the information available for few-shot learning through a training objective specifically designed to work without target labels.
neurips-2019-learning-to-learn-by-self-c.tldr: Self-Critique and Adapt learns a label-free loss that uses unlabeled target examples to improve few-shot adaptation.

paragraphs: Novelty detection concerns identifying observations that depart from familiar data. This paper develops a general neural framework for the task around a multivariate extension of the quantile function. Quantiles provide a way to describe positions within a distribution; extending that idea to multiple variables supplies the organizing principle for the proposed approach.

The framework brings together and extends a range of classical and recent novelty-detection algorithms. It also creates a route for using progress in flow-based neural density estimation. These connections matter because the contribution is broader than a single isolated detector: it provides a common formulation through which existing methods and newer density models can be related.

To make the framework practical, the authors adapt the multiple gradient descent algorithm and obtain an efficient end-to-end implementation described as free of tuning hyperparameters. Extensive experiments on several real datasets support its effectiveness against state-of-the-art alternatives. The stated findings combine a unifying mathematical framework with an implemented training procedure and empirical evidence that the resulting detector is useful.
neurips-2019-multivariate-triangular-qua.tldr: A multivariate quantile framework unifies novelty detectors and enables an efficient neural implementation without tuning hyperparameters.

paragraphs: Some classification methods deliberately produce randomized decisions. Such classifiers can arise when training must satisfy constraints involving fairness, churn, or custom losses. Although the randomness can be useful for constructing a solution, it can also make that solution difficult to use in practice. This paper asks how closely a deterministic classifier can approximate a stochastic one.

The authors compare several approaches to removing prediction randomness and establish both lower and upper bounds. These bounds address complementary questions: what approximation quality a method can achieve, and what limits constrain the task. The theoretical focus is therefore the relationship between the original randomized classifier and a replacement that makes deterministic decisions.

The experimental study considers more than approximation quality alone. It also examines how well each approach handles the practical issues that made randomness undesirable in the first place. This distinction matters because faithfully matching a stochastic classifier and providing a useful deterministic replacement are related but separate goals. The paper evaluates the advantages and disadvantages of the methods through both perspectives.
neurips-2019-on-making-stochastic-classi.tldr: The paper bounds and empirically compares ways to replace randomized classifiers with deterministic approximations.

paragraphs: Pure exploration bandit problems concern gathering enough observations to identify a satisfactory answer. This paper studies cases where several answers can be correct. The central question is sample complexity: how many observations are needed to complete the identification task when the learner has a choice among acceptable outcomes.

The authors derive a lower bound using a new argument based on a game equilibrium. They also explain why the existing Track-and-Stop algorithm achieves asymptotically optimal sample complexity in single-answer problems, connecting that result to continuity and convexity properties. This analysis identifies mathematical structure that supports efficient exploration when there is only one correct answer.

Moving to multiple correct answers removes the relevant convexity property, so the single-answer reasoning does not directly carry over. The paper develops an extension of Track-and-Stop that handles this setting and asymptotically matches the new lower bound. The result establishes both a fundamental sampling limit and an algorithm that reaches it asymptotically despite the changed structure of the answer space.
neurips-2019-pure-exploration-with-multi.tldr: An extension of Track-and-Stop achieves asymptotically optimal sampling when a bandit exploration problem has multiple correct answers.

paragraphs: This paper asks how unlabeled examples contribute to learning when the assumed data distribution can be adversarially perturbed. It joins semi-supervised learning, which uses labeled and unlabeled data, with distributionally robust learning. The resulting framework studies incomplete labeling and distributional uncertainty together, allowing their interaction to be analyzed within one learning problem.

The authors develop a generalization theory using new complexity measures, including adversarial and semi-supervised extensions of Rademacher complexity. Their analysis quantifies the role of unlabeled data under a condition more general than those used in existing semi-supervised theory. This provides a theoretical account of how unlabeled information enters generalization in the robust setting.

The paper also proposes an algorithm combining distributionally robust learning with expectation-maximization and establishes a convergence-rate guarantee. Implemented with deep neural networks, the method performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches on several real-world benchmarks. The contributions thus connect a theoretical treatment of unlabeled data with a concrete optimization procedure and empirical evidence of competitive performance.
neurips-2019-robustness-to-adversarial-p.tldr: A unified robust semi-supervised framework quantifies the role of unlabeled data and supports a convergent, empirically competitive algorithm.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to choose experiments for learning causal graphs with a tree structure. It assumes observational data is effectively unlimited while interventions are expensive. A Bayesian prior is updated after each experiment, and the next intervention is selected adaptively from what has already been learned.

The authors show that information-greedy choices can require exponentially more interventions in this setting. They instead propose using a graph centrality measure to guide experimentation. When infinite interventional data is available, their algorithm needs at most twice the minimum achievable number of interventions. This guarantee connects experimental efficiency to the tree’s structure rather than relying solely on immediate information gain.

The algorithm and theory are also adapted to interventions that yield finitely many samples. Further extensions cover nodes that cannot be intervened on, interventions scheduled in batches, and fully adaptive experiments returning one sample each. Simulations with finite interventional data show improvements over several adaptive baselines, supporting the practical value of the structural approach beyond the idealized infinite-data setting.
neurips-2019-sample-efficient-active-lea.tldr: A graph-based adaptive strategy learns causal trees efficiently, with a factor-two intervention guarantee in the infinite-interventional-data setting.

paragraphs: Large distributed datasets often contain key-value pairs, with each key’s frequency defined by the sum of its values. Some statistics weight keys through concave sublinear functions, such as capping or logarithms, to reduce the dominance of high-frequency keys. Computing useful samples for these statistics can be expensive if all frequencies must first be fully aggregated.

The paper introduces composable sampling sketches tailored to any concave sublinear function of frequency. These compact summaries support sampling without requiring the costly aggregate-then-sample workflow described in the paper. Their composability is particularly relevant to distributed data, where information from separate parts of the dataset must be brought together.

The sketch size is close to the desired number of sampled keys. The resulting samples also have estimation guarantees close to those of an ideal sample of equal size drawn from fully aggregated data. Experiments demonstrate simplicity and effectiveness. The contribution is therefore a compact sampling mechanism that approaches the statistical quality of aggregation-based sampling while addressing the cost of preparing that sample.
neurips-2019-sampling-sketches-for-conca.tldr: Composable sketches efficiently sample frequency-weighted keys with estimation guarantees close to ideal sampling from fully aggregated data.

paragraphs: Kernel dimensionality reduction captures nonlinear relationships, but its resulting features can be difficult to interpret. Interpretable kernel dimensionality reduction changes the order of operations: it projects the original inputs before applying the kernel mapping. The projection matrix then shows how original features combine linearly, giving the reduced representation a direct connection to the input variables.

This formulation creates a difficult nonconvex optimization problem over a constrained space. An iterative spectral method had offered an efficient approach, but its theoretical guarantees covered only the Gaussian kernel. The paper expands those guarantees to an entire family of kernels, widening the range of problems for which the method has theoretical support.

For each kernel in the identified family, the authors establish a surrogate matrix whose dominant eigenvectors form the optimal projection. This provides the spectral structure needed to extend the method across different interpretable reduction applications sharing the objective. The contribution links interpretability with a broader computational tool, enabling applications across learning settings while retaining the stated kernel-family qualification.
neurips-2019-solving-interpretable-kerne.tldr: The paper extends an iterative spectral solver’s guarantees to a broader kernel family for interpretable dimensionality reduction.

paragraphs: The paper introduces the thermodynamic variational objective, or TVO, as a training objective for deep generative models with continuous or discrete variables. Its central idea connects variational inference with thermodynamic integration, bringing these two approaches together to guide learning.

This connection produces a tighter lower bound on the log marginal likelihood than the standard evidence lower bound, known as the ELBO. The marginal likelihood measures how well a model accounts for observed data. A tighter bound gives training a closer approximation to this quantity, while the authors state that the TVO retains the ELBO’s broad applicability.

The authors also provide a computationally efficient estimator for the gradients needed to optimize the TVO. It supports continuous, discrete, and non-reparameterizable distributions. They show that objectives used in variational inference, variational autoencoders, wake sleep, and inference compilation fit within the TVO as special cases.

Experiments apply the objective to both discrete and continuous deep generative models. The authors report state-of-the-art learning for models and inference networks, providing empirical support for the framework’s usefulness alongside its unifying mathematical connection.
neurips-2019-the-thermodynamic-variation.tldr: The TVO connects variational inference and thermodynamic integration to provide a tighter learning bound and unify several existing training objectives.

paragraphs: Recurrent networks trained on neuroscience-inspired tasks are often compared with brain activity to infer how brain regions compute. This paper asks what such comparisons can establish. In particular, it examines whether learning the same task produces similar low-dimensional dynamics across network architectures, or whether architecture strongly shapes the resulting patterns.

The authors train thousands of recurrent networks and analyze their dynamics using canonical correlation analysis and nonlinear dynamical systems methods. They find that the geometry of the dynamics can depend strongly on architecture. They also observe substantial mismatches between geometric similarity measured by canonical correlation analysis and similarity of network function, making that comparison an uncertain guide to computation.

At the same time, a more structural description often appears shared across architectures. Fixed points, transitions, limit cycles, and local linearized dynamics can form a common computational scaffold despite differing geometry. The findings support distinguishing geometric resemblance from underlying dynamical organization when interpreting model-to-brain comparisons, with the observed commonality described as frequent rather than an unconditional property of all networks.
neurips-2019-universality-and-individual.tldr: Recurrent networks can share underlying computational structure despite architecture-dependent dynamics and misleading geometric similarity measures.

paragraphs: Policy evaluation estimates how well a fixed decision-making policy performs. Smooth nonlinear approximators, including neural networks, provide richer models than linear approximators for this task. This paper addresses the slow convergence associated with traditional two-timescale stochastic approximation methods, focusing on an offline setting with an already observed trajectory of m state-action pairs.

The authors express policy evaluation as a finite-sum primal-dual optimization problem. The primal part is nonconvex, while the dual part is strongly concave. They then propose a primal-dual gradient algorithm that uses a single timescale and variance reduction. The reformulation provides the structure for analyzing optimization with nonlinear approximation over the fixed trajectory.

The algorithm reaches an ε-stationary point using O(m/ε) gradient-oracle calls in expectation. A stationary-point guarantee describes progress toward a point with small optimization residual rather than establishing a global optimum for the nonconvex problem. The stated result gives an explicit computational bound in terms of the trajectory length and desired stationarity level for this offline policy-evaluation formulation.
neurips-2019-variance-reduced-policy-eva.tldr: A single-timescale variance-reduced algorithm evaluates policies with smooth nonlinear approximators using O(m/ε) expected gradient calls to reach stationarity.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can generate additional experience for reinforcement learning, but its errors can bias policy training. This paper studies how much to trust model-generated data. It first analyzes an algorithm with a step-by-step improvement guarantee, then examines why that analysis can be too pessimistic to guide effective model use in practice.

The initial analysis favors real data collected under other policies over synthetic data generated under the current policy. Incorporating an empirical estimate of model generalization provides a way to justify using the model. Motivated by this reasoning, the authors propose short simulated rollouts that begin from real data, making limited model use the core of the practical procedure.

The reported experiments show better sample efficiency than prior model-based methods and eventual performance matching the best model-free algorithms. The approach also handles horizons where other model-based methods fail. These findings support short rollouts from real experience as a useful balance between obtaining extra training data and controlling the consequences of model error in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2019-when-to-trust-your-model-mo.tldr: Short model-generated rollouts starting from real data improve sample efficiency while preserving strong eventual policy performance in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Wide neural networks with random weights and biases can correspond to Gaussian processes, giving a probabilistic description of their outputs across inputs. This paper extends that correspondence beyond previously studied fully connected and convolutional cases. Its result covers a broad range of modern feed-forward and recurrent architectures within a shared mathematical framework.

The supported components include multilayer perceptrons, recurrent units such as LSTMs and GRUs, ordinary and graph convolutions, pooling, skip connections, attention, and batch or layer normalization. The authors introduce a language for expressing neural-network computations, and the theorem encompasses networks expressible in that language. This makes the scope precise through the computation framework rather than through a short list of architectures.

The paper also serves as a tutorial on tensor programs, the technique underlying the result. Implementations of Gaussian-process kernels are provided for a simple RNN, a GRU, a transformer, and a network using batch normalization with ReLU. Together, the theory and implementations broaden the range of random wide networks that can be understood through Gaussian-process descriptions.
neurips-2019-wide-feedforward-or-recurre.tldr: Tensor programs extend the Gaussian-process correspondence for random wide networks to a broad range of feed-forward and recurrent architectures.
